title: Paragraph Completion
tagline: Year 2 — Choosing the final sentence that fits the logic and tone of a paragraph

introduction.overview: In a paragraph-completion question you read a short paragraph with the last sentence missing and choose the option that completes it best. The right choice continues the idea of the paragraph, matches its tone, and fits the logical signal given by the last words (therefore, however, as a result, finally). Wrong options are usually off-topic, contradictory, too extreme or repeat the paragraph without adding anything.
introduction.placementRelevance: Paragraph completion questions are commonly asked in the verbal ability section of company aptitude rounds and help build reading comprehension skill.
introduction.realWorldContext: Writing a conclusion to an email or report, and checking that it follows from the argument, uses this skill.

learningObjectives: Identify the main idea of a short paragraph
Use transition signals (however, therefore, as a result) to predict the type of ending
Reject off-topic, contradictory and extreme options
Match the tone and scope of the paragraph
Check that the completed paragraph flows logically

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: A paragraph has one main idea. Transition words tell you the direction: addition (also), contrast (however), result (so, therefore, as a result), sequence (finally).

coreDefinitions: Main idea: the central point of the paragraph.
Transition word: a word that links ideas and signals the relationship (however, therefore).
Continuation: a sentence that extends the idea of the paragraph.
Conclusion: a closing sentence that follows from the earlier ones.
Off-topic option: one that changes the subject.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: The best ending follows from what came before. After a cause, the ending states the result. After a problem, it states a response or a consequence. After "however", it states a contrast. Predict the kind of sentence, then find the option that matches.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Summarise the paragraph in one line, look at the last signal word, predict the ending, and check each option for relevance, direction and tone.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Signal: result
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: So / therefore / as a result / hence → a consequence
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: Plastic harms animals → many cities have banned it

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Signal: contrast
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: However / yet / although → an opposite idea
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: Critics said it would hurt the poor → the government claimed welfare benefits

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Signal: sequence
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Finally / suddenly / on the day → the next event in the story
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: Studied for years → finally got admission

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Scope check
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: The ending must match the scope (not extreme, not unrelated)

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Repetition check
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: The ending must add something, not repeat

mainNarrative: Read the paragraph and put its idea in a single line. "Regular exercise keeps the body fit and improves mood and sleep" leads to a recommendation: therefore everyone should make exercise part of daily life.

Use the signal word. In "Many students think cramming is the best way to study. Research shows, however, that ___", the word however introduces a contrast: understanding concepts leads to better long-term learning.
For narrative paragraphs, continue the story. "The library was silent… Suddenly ___" needs an event that interrupts the silence: a phone rang loudly.

Reject options that are off-topic, extreme or contradictory. After "Early humans learned to grow crops. This change… ___", the ending should explain its effect: it allowed people to settle in one place and form villages.
Reread the paragraph with your choice to check that it flows and that the tone is consistent.

deepDiveAspects.title: Parallel structure at the end
deepDiveAspects.content: If the paragraph lists benefits, the ending may add another benefit. If it states a problem, the ending may offer a solution. Look at the shape of the paragraph.

deepDiveAspects.title: Extreme options
deepDiveAspects.content: Words like always, never, all and nobody make an option risky. Prefer measured statements unless the paragraph is itself extreme.

solvedExamples.title: Result
solvedExamples.question: Plastic bags take hundreds of years to decay. They also harm animals that eat them. Many cities have therefore ___
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: Therefore signals a response to the problem.

solvedExamples.title: Contrast
solvedExamples.question: Many students think that cramming is the best way to study. Research shows, however, that ___
solvedExamples.finalAnswer: understanding concepts leads to better long-term learning.

solvedExamples.title: Narrative
solvedExamples.question: The library was silent. Students were bent over their books. Suddenly ___
solvedExamples.conceptOrFormula: An event that breaks the silence.
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The event contrasts with the silence.

traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Summarise the paragraph, read the signal word, predict the ending, then pick the closest option.

commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Choosing a plausible but wrong direction.
The option says the same thing.
A casual end to a formal paragraph.

placementTips.questionSelectionAdvice: Predict the ending in your own words.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: Signal words make most questions easy.
